source: Wikipedia articles that record a specific event on one atlas island

rows.title: The quarries drowned
rows.evidence: The great storm of 1850 flooded the majority of the quarries and, as the islanders were unable to extract the floodwater, most were abandoned.
rows.summary: In 1850 a storm drove the sea into most of the slate quarries on Easdale. The island could not get the water out again, and most of the workings were given up. The old cuttings are still pools.

rows.title: An experimental camp
rows.evidence: The island was the location of an experimental camp in 1907 that preceded the publication of Scouting for Boys and The Scout magazine in 1908.
rows.summary: In 1907 Brownsea Island was the site of a trial camp for boys. The account of the island says that camp came before Scouting for Boys and The Scout magazine, both published in 1908.

rows.title: Europe's first dark sanctuary
rows.evidence: In 2023, the island became the first site in Europe to be awarded International Dark Sky Sanctuary certification.
rows.summary: In 2023 Bardsey became the first place in Europe named an International Dark Sky Sanctuary. The island's account records the award.

rows.title: The wall made an island
rows.evidence: Much of the silt now scoured from the river course was deposited on the North Bull, and a true island began to emerge, with people venturing out to the growing beach.
rows.reject_reason: The silt story is how the island formed, not one strange event
rows.summary: The Bull Wall across Dublin Bay was finished in 1825. Silt the tide no longer left in the river settled on the North Bull, and over the next decades a sandbank grew into an island that people walked out to.

rows.title: Twenty hours under water
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph by Derek Robertson, derivative work by Cactus.man, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: It was built between 1807 and 1810 by Robert Stevenson on the Bell Rock (also known as Inchcape) in the North Sea, 11 miles (18 km) east of the Firth of Tay.
rows.reject_reason: Ordinary building history, not an unusual event
rows.summary: Robert Stevenson built a lighthouse on Inchcape, the Bell Rock, between 1807 and 1810. The rock lies under the sea except for a few hours at low tide, and for most of each day it is covered by as much as twelve feet of water, so the masons lived on a ship a mile off and rowed in when the stone showed.
rows.image_note: The Bell Rock lighthouse on Inchcape
rows.image_alt: The Bell Rock lighthouse on Inchcape

rows.title: Lost on a bet
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph by Eusebius, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: The Stewarts' relative King James VI of Scotland visited the castle, and a drunken bet, around 1620, resulted in the castle passing to Clan Campbell.
rows.summary: Around 1620, after a visit from James VI, Castle Stalker passed from the Stewarts to Clan Campbell on a drunken bet. The castle stands on its own tidal rock.

rows.title: The border crosses the rock
rows.evidence: Its rocky southern foreshore marks the boundary between England and Wales.
rows.reject_reason: The foreshore is a boundary, not an event
rows.summary: Denny Island is a small rock in the Severn. Its southern foreshore is the boundary between England and Wales, and above high water the island is reckoned to Monmouthshire.

rows.title: An invitation to move
rows.evidence: In 2019, islanders wrote open letters to the United States and Australia, asking people to consider moving to the island.
rows.summary: In 2019 the people of Arranmore wrote open letters to the United States and Australia and asked anyone looking for more room to come and live on the island.

rows.title: A tender drawn by a horse
rows.evidence: On the first visit with Prince Albert on 8 August 1854, the Royal couple rode on a horse-drawn railway tender.
rows.summary: Queen Victoria used the Alderney railway on three visits. On the first, with Prince Albert, on 8 August 1854, they rode a tender pulled by a horse.

rows.title: The first signal over open sea
rows.evidence: On 13 May 1897, a 22-year-old Italian inventor named Guglielmo Marconi, assisted by a Cardiff Post Office engineer named George Kemp, transmitted the first Wireless signals over open sea from Flat Holm to Lavernock Point near Penarth, Wales.
rows.summary: On 13 May 1897 Guglielmo Marconi sent the first wireless signals across open water, from Flat Holm to Lavernock Point. George Kemp, a Cardiff Post Office engineer, was with him.

rows.title: Fifteen million watched the stack
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph by Babs64, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: From 8 to 9 July 1967, an ascent featured in The Great Climb, a live BBC three-night outside broadcast, which had around 15 million viewers.
rows.summary: The Old Man of Hoy is a sea stack on Hoy, first climbed in 1966. From 8 to 9 July 1967 the BBC showed a climb of it live across three nights, and about fifteen million people watched.
rows.image_note: The Old Man of Hoy, a sea stack on Hoy
rows.image_alt: The Old Man of Hoy, a sea stack on Hoy

rows.title: A king chosen by the island
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph by bminish, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: In keeping with a long-standing tradition, a "king" is chosen by consensus of the islanders.
rows.reject_reason: An ongoing custom, not a news event
rows.summary: Tory Island chooses a king by agreement among the people who live there. The post has no legal power. The painter Patsy Dan Rodgers held it from the 1990s until his death on 19 October 2018.

rows.title: Built to look like a warship
rows.evidence: The concrete buildings make the island look (from a distance) like a battleship.
rows.reject_reason: The island looks like a battleship; that is an appearance, not an event
rows.summary: Wartime concrete on Inchmickery was laid out so that, from a distance, the island reads as a battleship. Much of that superstructure is still standing.

rows.title: Shut for the grandgore
rows.evidence: In 1497, the island was (along with Inchgarvie, a few miles away) used as an isolated refuge for victims of 'grandgore' (also spelled 'glandgore'), an old Scots name for 'syphilis', in Edinburgh.
rows.summary: In 1497 Edinburgh used Inchkeith as a place apart for people with the grandgore, the old name for syphilis. Inchgarvie, a few miles away, was used in the same way.

rows.title: Silver under the floor
rows.evidence: The important early medieval St Ninian's Isle Treasure of metalwork, mostly in silver, was discovered under the church floor in 1958.
rows.summary: In 1958 a hoard of early medieval silver, bowls and jewellery, was found under a stone slab in the floor of the church on St Ninian's Isle. The pieces are dated to about 750–825.

rows.title: Earth from under London
rows.evidence: In September 2012 it was announced that work had begun on the Wallasea Island Wild Coast Project under which around 4.5 million tonnes of earth were transported to Wallasea Island, via over 1500 separate trips, many by rail and water, to help create the nature reserve from London's Crossrail tunnel (Elizabeth line) excavation.
rows.summary: In September 2012 work began on moving about 4.5 million tonnes of earth to Wallasea Island, in more than 1,500 trips, many by rail and water. The earth came out of the Crossrail tunnels under London and was used to make a wetland on the island.

rows.title: A whale that could not turn
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph by John Phillips, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: In 1835 a whale measuring 24 metres (79 ft) with a lower jaw of 7 metres (23 ft) was stranded having become trapped in shallow water and unable to reverse out.
rows.summary: The Clachan Bridge joins Seil to the mainland across a narrow sound, and whales are sometimes trapped in that channel. In 1835 one measuring 24 metres stuck in the shallows and could not back out. In 1837, 192 pilot whales were caught in the same way.
rows.image_note: The Clachan Bridge, which links Seil to the mainland
rows.image_alt: The Clachan Bridge, which links Seil to the mainland

rows.title: The island changed hands
rows.evidence: In March 2018 the Scottish Land Fund pledged £4.4 million towards a community buyout of the island, and the North West Mull Community Woodland Company took ownership of the island on 21 June 2018.
rows.reject_reason: The 2018 community buyout is an ordinary transfer, not a strange event
rows.summary: On 21 June 2018 a community company took ownership of Ulva. The Scottish Land Fund had pledged £4.4 million toward the purchase that March. The island once had more than 800 people; by May 2019 the number recorded was five.

rows.title: Pigs put out for the eggs
rows.evidence: Pigs were loosed in the Spring on the Horse for many years, and they fed on the bird's eggs.
rows.reject_reason: Pigs loosed to eat eggs is a practice, not one event
rows.summary: For many years pigs were turned loose on the Horse of Copinsay each spring. The account of Copinsay says they fed on the eggs of the birds there.

rows.title: Out in a servant's clothes
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph by Debbynash68, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: On the night she finally successfully escaped, she dressed as a servant, Willie Douglas stole the keys, and Marie Courcelles let her walk out of the castle.
rows.summary: Lochleven Castle stands on an island in Loch Leven. Mary, Queen of Scots, was held there from 17 June 1567. On the night of 2 May 1568 she dressed as a servant, the keys were taken, and she was rowed off the island.
rows.image_note: Lochleven Castle, on an island in Loch Leven
rows.image_alt: Lochleven Castle, on an island in Loch Leven

rows.title: Footprints in the rock
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph by Terryballard, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: In 1992, a Swiss geology student, Iwan Stössel, discovered fossilised tetrapod trackways, footprints preserved in Devonian rocks, on the north coast of the island.
rows.summary: In 1992 a Swiss geology student, Iwan Stössel, found fossil footprints on the north coast of Valentia. They are the tracks of an early vertebrate, left in Devonian mud about 385 million years ago.

rows.title: Dark for five years
rows.evidence: The light shone without a break from 1844 until a fire in 1954 shut down operations for five years.
rows.summary: The Skerryvore light burned without a break from 1844 until a fire in 1954. The lighthouse account says the light then stayed out for five years.

rows.title: Christmas on 6 January
rows.evidence: Foula is now one day ahead of the Julian calendar and 12 days behind the Gregorian, observing Christmas Day on 6 January Gregorian and New Year on 13 January Gregorian.
rows.reject_reason: Old-style Christmas dates are a custom, not a news event
rows.summary: Foula stayed on the Julian calendar when the rest of Britain moved to the Gregorian calendar in 1752. The island now keeps Christmas on 6 January and New Year on 13 January.

rows.title: Wallabies until 1910
rows.evidence: When Prince Gebhard Fürst Blücher von Wahlstatt and Princess Blücher leased the island from the British government in 1889, he introduced a colony of red-necked wallabies to the island, which lasted until 1910.
rows.summary: In 1889, under a lease from the British government, red-necked wallabies were brought to Herm. They remained on the island until 1910.

rows.title: The widow who was queen
rows.evidence: The islanders had a parliament, similar to that of St Kilda, which met daily, and the oldest widow on the island was considered its "Queen".
rows.reject_reason: The daily parliament and widow queen are a custom, not a news event
rows.summary: Handa kept a parliament that met every day, and the oldest widow was treated as the island's queen. After the potato famine of 1847 the people left for Nova Scotia.

rows.title: All professed smugglers
rows.evidence: An inspector who visited the island's school in 1824 described the inhabitants of Stroma as "all professed smugglers".
rows.summary: In 1824 a school inspector wrote that the people of Stroma all professed to be smugglers. When that trade was put down, the population fell through the first half of the nineteenth century.
